newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Strong dlr seen easing HK inflation, hurting export.
newsitem.headline: Strong dlr seen easing HK inflation, hurting export.

text.p: The continued strength of the U.S. dollar would help ease inflationary pressures in Hong Kong, but would erode the relative price competitiveness of local products in world markets, Hang Seng Bank said on Tuesday.

As the U.S. dollar appreciated in foreign exchange markets, the Hong Kong dollar, which is pegged at HK$7.8 to US$1.0, also rose 50 percent against the yen and 23 percent against the mark over the past 22 months, the bank said in an economic report.
With the U.S. unit likely to remain strong in the coming months, the corresponding strength of the Hong Kong dollar would ease inflationary pressure by lowering import prices, it said.

Import inflation contributed only 1.4 percentage points to the seven percent increase in the Hang Seng Consumer Price Index last year, and inflation was likely to remain moderate at seven percent this year despite a rebound in the economy, it said.

Last year's 1.2 percent drop in import prices also helped partially reduce export prices by holding down raw material import costs, although export prices only fell 0.3 percent due to the effect of other input costs, the bank said.
The ratio of export prices to import prices did improve one percent last year and further improvement was likely near term.
"However, whether Hong Kong's trade position will improve depends on the extent that price changes are offset by volume changes," the bank said.
"As the appreciation of the local currency would erode the relative price competitiveness of local products in world markets, slower growth in export volume can be expected."
Exports to Japan and Europe would be more affected by the strong dollar, but exports to the United States and China would not be unscathed either, it warned.
Hong Kong's total export volume growth might at best average only 10 percent in 1997, the bank said.
Any deceleration in export growth would dampen domestic consumption and investment, reducing overall economic growth in Hong Kong, it added.
